title: Fast kinematics modeling for conjunction with lens image modeling

en.text: How fast is the universe expanding? The question, captured by the Hubble constant (H0), sits at the center of one of the sharpest tensions in modern cosmology: the value inferred from the early universe and the value measured directly in the nearby universe disagree by more than statistics can explain. Time-delay cosmography, which uses gravitational lensing, offers an independent route to H0 that does not lean on the traditional distance ladder — which is exactly what makes it valuable.

The idea is elegant: a foreground galaxy bends the light of a background quasar into multiple images, and because those images trace different paths, their light arrives days to months apart. Match that time delay to a model of the lens galaxy's mass and you can back out a cosmic distance scale, and from it H0. The catch is degeneracy. Lensing suffers from the mass-sheet degeneracy: many different mass distributions reproduce almost the same image, and the imaging data alone cannot tell them apart. Breaking that degeneracy requires an independent constraint — the stellar kinematics of the lens galaxy, essentially how fast its stars are moving.

The problem is that kinematics modeling is slow. To solve the kinematics and the imaging self-consistently, you predict the galaxy's velocity field with a physics code like JAM (Jeans Anisotropic Modeling), and inside an MCMC sampler that code must be recomputed for every single likelihood evaluation. One call takes on the order of fifteen seconds; multiplied over the hundreds of thousands of evaluations a chain needs, jointly exploring the lensing and kinematics parameter spaces becomes computationally prohibitive, so in practice modelers fall back to fitting the two pieces separately. This paper's contribution, SKiNN (Stellar Kinematics Neural Network), targets exactly that bottleneck: train a network to imitate JAM's output, and the slowest step becomes a single forward pass.

en.caption: Figure 1. Where SKiNN fits in a joint modeling framework. The top row (blue) is traditional lens modeling: a model for the source, lens mass, and lens light builds an image that is compared to the imaging data, giving chi-squared_lens. The bottom row (orange) is SKiNN: lens mass, lens light, and kinematics parameters feed a network that outputs a vrms velocity image, compared to the kinematic data to give chi-squared_kin. The combined chi-squared_tot is minimized to optimize the whole model jointly. SKiNN replaces only the kinematics piece; the rest of the framework's physics is untouched.

en.text: Paper (NeurIPS 2022): https://neurips.cc/virtual/2022/57003
Code: https://github.com/mattgomer/SKiNN
Why kinematics modeling is the bottleneck

Spherical Jeans models, the traditional shortcut, are too crude for spatially resolved data and are not self-consistent with the elliptical mass models used in lensing. As instruments like JWST deliver spatially resolved kinematics of lens galaxies, the natural next step is axisymmetric modeling with a code like JAM. But JAM is expensive, and the expense compounds: it lives in the innermost loop of the likelihood evaluation, and an MCMC chain can call that loop hundreds of thousands of times. The cost is not running it once; it is running it again and again.

The key observation is that JAM, though slow, is deterministic and fully calculable. That makes it a good candidate for emulation: generate a batch of JAM outputs, and train a neural network to approximate the mapping. Training is a one-time cost; afterwards each inference is cheap. Importantly, the network does not replace the physics of the overall model — it replaces only the parameters-to-velocity-image computation, while everything around it stays physical.
How SKiNN is built

Formally, SKiNN is a function Psi-theta that maps an 8-dimensional vector of galaxy parameters to a d x d image of vrms (the quadrature sum of velocity dispersion and rotational velocity). The eight inputs describe a Power-law Elliptical Mass Distribution (PEMD) plus an elliptical Sersic light profile — six shape parameters in total — together with the galaxy's inclination i and its orbital anisotropy beta. The architecture is convolutional: five blocks, each with two 2D convolutional layers followed by upsampling and a ReLU nonlinearity, for roughly 7.07 million trainable parameters. It is trained with a standard mean-squared-error loss and the Adam optimizer so that the network learns to reproduce JAM's output.

The training data is generated entirely by JAM: 5,000 input-output pairs, split 4,000 for training, 500 for validation, and 500 held out for testing. Each velocity image is 551 x 551 pixels, at higher resolution than real observations. A single JAM image takes about fifteen seconds to produce, which is precisely why emulation pays off. The network is implemented in PyTorch with PyTorch Lightning and trained on five Tesla P100 GPUs (16 GB each) in about a day. The parameter ranges are physically motivated rather than sampled arbitrarily.
About 300x faster, at under one percent error

Once trained, SKiNN turns a parameter vector into a velocity image in about 50 milliseconds on a single GPU, against roughly 15 seconds for JAM — about a 300x speedup (and the GPU is itself about 10x faster than a CPU here). The real question is whether that speed costs accuracy. The authors answer it by computing the per-pixel relative error on the 500 held-out test images.

en.caption: Figure 2. Two vrms images produced by SKiNN compared against JAM ground truth. The first two columns show SKiNN's prediction and the JAM truth; the third shows the per-pixel relative error, with the black circle marking the innermost two arcseconds, where real data is most constraining. Errors can reach a few percent in the outskirts, but inside the circle they stay below 1% almost everywhere; the histograms on the right confirm that the within-circle relative error concentrates within plus or minus one percent.

en.text: The reading is clear. Errors of a few percent do appear in the image outskirts, but those regions carry little constraining power anyway. In the innermost two arcseconds, where the data actually speaks, the emulation matches JAM to within plus or minus one percent for nearly every pixel. Averaged over whole images, the median absolute error across the 500 test images is about 0.47%, and the 90th percentile is about 1.1% — both comfortably below the roughly 2%-or-greater systematic uncertainty typical of real velocity measurements. In other words, the emulation error is swamped by observational noise, so it should not dominate the science.

en.caption: Table 1. Speed and accuracy of SKiNN versus JAM for a single vrms image.

en.text: Why it matters, and where it stops

By turning the slowest step of joint modeling into a cheap forward pass, SKiNN makes it computationally feasible, for the first time, to fit gravitational lensing and spatially resolved kinematics together — and it is precisely the kinematic constraint that corrects the largest source of uncertainty in H0 measurements. The authors are candid about the scope: this is a proof-of-concept. There is no formal ablation table; performance is characterized by the per-pixel error distribution on the test set, the emulator is only valid within the sampled parameter ranges, and the outskirts of the image do carry larger errors.

Perhaps the more transferable idea is the strategy itself: when a model contains an expensive-but-calculable component, you can train a network to emulate that one piece while keeping the surrounding physics intact. You buy the speed of a neural network without giving up the interpretability of the full physical model. That 'replace only the slowest block' pattern seems likely to carry over to many scientific modeling problems well beyond astrophysics.

zh.text: 宇宙到底膨胀得有多快？这个用哈勃常数（Hubble constant, H0）刻画的问题，如今是天文学里最受关注的争论之一：用早期宇宙推算出的 H0 和用近邻宇宙直接测量出的 H0 对不上，差距已经无法用统计误差解释。引力透镜时间延迟（time-delay cosmography）提供了一条独立的测量路线，它不依赖传统的距离阶梯，因此格外重要。

它的原理是：一个前景星系的引力把背景类星体的光弯折成多个像，不同像的光走过不同路径、到达时间相差几天到几个月；把这个时间延迟和星系质量模型对起来，就能反推出宇宙的尺度，进而得到 H0。问题在于，透镜本身存在“质量片退化”（mass-sheet degeneracy）等简并——很多不同的质量分布能拼出几乎一样的成像，单靠成像数据无法区分。要打破这种简并，就需要一份独立的约束：星系内恒星的运动学（kinematics），也就是恒星的速度弥散。

麻烦的是运动学建模太慢。要把运动学和成像放在一起自洽求解，需要用 JAM 这类基于物理的轴对称动力学代码来预测速度场，而在 MCMC 采样里，每评估一次似然就要把 JAM 重新算一遍。单次计算就要十几秒，成千上万次叠加下来，联合探索透镜和运动学两个参数空间在计算上几乎不可行，实践中只能退而求其次，把两部分分开拟合。本文提出的 SKiNN（Stellar Kinematics Neural Network，恒星运动学神经网络）正是针对这个瓶颈：用一个神经网络去“模仿”JAM 的输出，把最慢的一步换成一次前向推理。

zh.caption: 图1 SKiNN 在联合建模框架中的位置。上半部分（蓝色）是传统透镜建模：用源、透镜质量、透镜光的模型合成一张成像图，与成像数据比对得到 χ²_lens。下半部分（橙色）是 SKiNN：输入透镜质量、透镜光和运动学参数，直接输出一张 vrms 速度图，与运动学数据比对得到 χ²_kin。两者合成的 χ²_tot 被联合最小化，从而对整个模型同时优化。SKiNN 只替换了运动学这一块，框架其余部分的物理保持不变。

zh.text: 论文链接（NeurIPS 2022）：https://neurips.cc/virtual/2022/57003
代码仓库：https://github.com/mattgomer/SKiNN
为什么运动学建模会成为瓶颈
过去用球对称的 Jeans 模型来近似星系动力学，对新数据来说太粗糙，而且和透镜里用的椭圆质量模型并不自洽。随着 JWST 等望远镜带来空间分辨的运动学数据，自然的下一步是用 JAM 这类轴对称模型来自洽建模。但 JAM 的代价很高：它必须嵌在似然评估的最内层循环里被反复调用，而 MCMC 动辄需要几十万次评估。换句话说，慢的不是算一次，而是要算很多很多次。
本文的关键判断是：JAM 虽然慢，但它是可计算、有确定输入输出的。既然如此，就可以用一批 JAM 生成的样本训练一个神经网络去逼近这个映射。训练是一次性的开销，训练好之后每次推理都很便宜。整个模型的物理并没有被神经网络取代——被替换的只是“把参数变成速度图”这一段纯计算，框架其余部分仍然是原来的物理。
SKiNN 是怎么设计的

形式上，SKiNN 是一个函数 Ψθ，把一个 8 维的星系参数向量映射成一张 d×d 的 vrms 图（vrms 是速度弥散与转动速度的平方和）。这 8 个输入描述了一个幂律椭圆质量分布（Power-law Elliptical Mass Distribution, PEMD）加上一个椭圆 Sérsic 光分布，共 6 个形状参数，再加上星系的倾角 i 和轨道各向异性 β。网络是一个卷积结构，共 5 个模块，每个模块包含两层二维卷积、一层上采样和 ReLU 非线性，最终约有 707 万个可训练参数。训练用标准的均方误差（MSE）损失和 Adam 优化器，让网络学着复刻 JAM 的输出。

训练数据完全由 JAM 生成，共 5000 个输入-输出对，其中 4000 个用于训练、500 个用于验证、500 个留作测试。每张速度图是 551×551 像素，分辨率高于真实观测数据。用 JAM 生成一张这样的图大约要 15 秒，这也从反面说明了为什么值得做仿真加速。网络用 PyTorch 加 PyTorch Lightning 实现，在 5 块 Tesla P100 GPU（每块 16 GB）上训练约一天。所有参数的取值范围都有物理动机，而不是随意采样。
速度提升 300 倍，精度损失不到 1%
训练完成后，SKiNN 在单块 GPU 上从参数向量生成一张速度图只需约 50 毫秒，相比 JAM 的约 15 秒，大约快了 300 倍（在 GPU 上又比 CPU 快约 10 倍）。真正关键的问题是：这么快，精度还够用吗？作者在 500 张留出的测试图上逐像素计算相对误差来回答。

zh.caption: 图2 两个由 SKiNN 生成的 vrms 图与 JAM 真值的对比。左两列分别是 SKiNN 预测和 JAM 真值，第三列是逐像素相对误差，黑色圆圈标出最内 2 角秒——真实数据约束力最强的区域。可以看到误差在图像外围可能达到几个百分点，但在圆圈内几乎处处小于 1%；最右列的直方图进一步显示，圆内相对误差集中分布在 ±1% 以内。

zh.text: 结论很清楚：图像外围的确会出现几个百分点的误差，但外围本身几乎不受真实数据约束，影响有限；而在最内 2 角秒这个数据真正说话的区域，误差对几乎所有像素都控制在 ±1% 以内。把整张图平均下来，500 张测试图的绝对误差中位数约为 0.47%，第 90 百分位约为 1.1%——两者都明显低于真实速度测量里通常 ≳2% 的系统不确定度。也就是说，仿真带来的误差被真实观测的噪声“淹没”了，不会成为科学结论的主要误差来源。

zh.caption: 表1 SKiNN 与 JAM 的速度和精度对比（单张 vrms 图）。
rows: 整图误差中位数 / 90 分位

zh.text: 意义与边界
SKiNN 把联合建模里最慢的一步换成了一次廉价的前向推理，让引力透镜与空间分辨运动学的联合拟合在计算上第一次变得可行——而正是运动学约束，能纠正 H0 测量里最大的一类不确定性。作者也如实说明了它的定位：这是一个概念验证（proof-of-concept），没有给出正式的消融表，性能由测试集上的逐像素误差分布刻画；仿真只在参数取样的既定范围内有效，外围区域的误差也确实更大。
更值得关注的也许是它背后的思路：当模型里存在“昂贵但可计算”的组件时，可以用一个神经网络仿真这一块，同时把周围的物理原样保留，既借到神经网络的速度，又不牺牲整体模型的物理可解释性。这种“只换最慢的一块”的策略，很可能迁移到天体物理之外的许多科学建模问题上。

en.text: How fast is the universe expanding? The question, captured by the Hubble constant (H0), sits at the center of one of the sharpest tensions in modern cosmology: the value inferred from the early universe and the value measured directly in the nearby universe disagree by more than statistics can explain. Time-delay cosmography, which uses gravitational lensing, offers an independent route to H0 that does not lean on the traditional distance ladder — which is exactly what makes it valuable.

The idea is elegant: a foreground galaxy bends the light of a background quasar into multiple images, and because those images trace different paths, their light arrives days to months apart. Match that time delay to a model of the lens galaxy's mass and you can back out a cosmic distance scale, and from it H0. The catch is degeneracy. Lensing suffers from the mass-sheet degeneracy: many different mass distributions reproduce almost the same image, and the imaging data alone cannot tell them apart. Breaking that degeneracy requires an independent constraint — the stellar kinematics of the lens galaxy, essentially how fast its stars are moving.

The problem is that kinematics modeling is slow. To solve the kinematics and the imaging self-consistently, you predict the galaxy's velocity field with a physics code like JAM (Jeans Anisotropic Modeling), and inside an MCMC sampler that code must be recomputed for every single likelihood evaluation. One call takes on the order of fifteen seconds; multiplied over the hundreds of thousands of evaluations a chain needs, jointly exploring the lensing and kinematics parameter spaces becomes computationally prohibitive, so in practice modelers fall back to fitting the two pieces separately. This paper's contribution, SKiNN (Stellar Kinematics Neural Network), targets exactly that bottleneck: train a network to imitate JAM's output, and the slowest step becomes a single forward pass.

en.caption: Figure 1. Where SKiNN fits in a joint modeling framework. The top row (blue) is traditional lens modeling: a model for the source, lens mass, and lens light builds an image that is compared to the imaging data, giving chi-squared_lens. The bottom row (orange) is SKiNN: lens mass, lens light, and kinematics parameters feed a network that outputs a vrms velocity image, compared to the kinematic data to give chi-squared_kin. The combined chi-squared_tot is minimized to optimize the whole model jointly. SKiNN replaces only the kinematics piece; the rest of the framework's physics is untouched.

en.text: Paper (NeurIPS 2022): https://neurips.cc/virtual/2022/57003
Code: https://github.com/mattgomer/SKiNN

zh.caption: 图1 SKiNN 在联合建模框架中的位置。上半部分（蓝色）是传统透镜建模：用源、透镜质量、透镜光的模型合成一张成像图，与成像数据比对得到 χ²_lens。下半部分（橙色）是 SKiNN：输入透镜质量、透镜光和运动学参数，直接输出一张 vrms 速度图，与运动学数据比对得到 χ²_kin。两者合成的 χ²_tot 被联合最小化，从而对整个模型同时优化。SKiNN 只替换了运动学这一块，框架其余部分的物理保持不变。

zh.text: SKiNN 是怎么设计的

形式上，SKiNN 是一个函数 Ψθ，把一个 8 维的星系参数向量映射成一张 d×d 的 vrms 图（vrms 是速度弥散与转动速度的平方和）。这 8 个输入描述了一个幂律椭圆质量分布（Power-law Elliptical Mass Distribution, PEMD）加上一个椭圆 Sérsic 光分布，共 6 个形状参数，再加上星系的倾角 i 和轨道各向异性 β。网络是一个卷积结构，共 5 个模块，每个模块包含两层二维卷积、一层上采样和 ReLU 非线性，最终约有 707 万个可训练参数。训练用标准的均方误差（MSE）损失和 Adam 优化器，让网络学着复刻 JAM 的输出。

训练数据完全由 JAM 生成，共 5000 个输入-输出对，其中 4000 个用于训练、500 个用于验证、500 个留作测试。每张速度图是 551×551 像素，分辨率高于真实观测数据。用 JAM 生成一张这样的图大约要 15 秒，这也从反面说明了为什么值得做仿真加速。网络用 PyTorch 加 PyTorch Lightning 实现，在 5 块 Tesla P100 GPU（每块 16 GB）上训练约一天。所有参数的取值范围都有物理动机，而不是随意采样。

en.title: NeurIPS 2022: Emulating the Slowest Step in Lensing Cosmography with a Neural Network
en.subtitle: SKiNN swaps a slow physics-based kinematics code for a CNN — about 300x faster, at sub-percent accuracy

zh.title: NeurIPS 2022 | 给星系动力学建模提速 300 倍，让哈勃常数测得更准
zh.subtitle: SKiNN：用一个卷积网络替换引力透镜宇宙学里最慢的物理计算，精度损失不到 1%

en.text: About 300x faster, at under one percent error

Once trained, SKiNN turns a parameter vector into a velocity image in about 50 milliseconds on a single GPU, against roughly 15 seconds for JAM — about a 300x speedup (and the GPU is itself about 10x faster than a CPU here). The real question is whether that speed costs accuracy. The authors answer it by computing the per-pixel relative error on the 500 held-out test images.

en.caption: Figure 2. Two vrms images produced by SKiNN compared against JAM ground truth. The first two columns show SKiNN's prediction and the JAM truth; the third shows the per-pixel relative error, with the black circle marking the innermost two arcseconds, where real data is most constraining. Errors can reach a few percent in the outskirts, but inside the circle they stay below 1% almost everywhere; the histograms on the right confirm that the within-circle relative error concentrates within plus or minus one percent.

en.text: The reading is clear. Errors of a few percent do appear in the image outskirts, but those regions carry little constraining power anyway. In the innermost two arcseconds, where the data actually speaks, the emulation matches JAM to within plus or minus one percent for nearly every pixel. Averaged over whole images, the median absolute error across the 500 test images is about 0.47%, and the 90th percentile is about 1.1% — both comfortably below the roughly 2%-or-greater systematic uncertainty typical of real velocity measurements. In other words, the emulation error is swamped by observational noise, so it should not dominate the science.

en.caption: Table 1. Speed and accuracy of SKiNN versus JAM for a single vrms image.

zh.text: 速度提升 300 倍，精度损失不到 1%
训练完成后，SKiNN 在单块 GPU 上从参数向量生成一张速度图只需约 50 毫秒，相比 JAM 的约 15 秒，大约快了 300 倍（在 GPU 上又比 CPU 快约 10 倍）。真正关键的问题是：这么快，精度还够用吗？作者在 500 张留出的测试图上逐像素计算相对误差来回答。

zh.caption: 图2 两个由 SKiNN 生成的 vrms 图与 JAM 真值的对比。左两列分别是 SKiNN 预测和 JAM 真值，第三列是逐像素相对误差，黑色圆圈标出最内 2 角秒——真实数据约束力最强的区域。可以看到误差在图像外围可能达到几个百分点，但在圆圈内几乎处处小于 1%；最右列的直方图进一步显示，圆内相对误差集中分布在 ±1% 以内。

zh.text: 结论很清楚：图像外围的确会出现几个百分点的误差，但外围本身几乎不受真实数据约束，影响有限；而在最内 2 角秒这个数据真正说话的区域，误差对几乎所有像素都控制在 ±1% 以内。把整张图平均下来，500 张测试图的绝对误差中位数约为 0.47%，第 90 百分位约为 1.1%——两者都明显低于真实速度测量里通常 ≳2% 的系统不确定度。也就是说，仿真带来的误差被真实观测的噪声“淹没”了，不会成为科学结论的主要误差来源。

zh.caption: 表1 SKiNN 与 JAM 的速度和精度对比（单张 vrms 图）。
rows: 整图误差中位数 / 90 分位

en.caption: Figure 1. Where SKiNN fits in a joint modeling framework. The top row (blue) is traditional lens modeling: a model for the source, lens mass, and lens light builds an image that is compared to the imaging data, giving chi-squared_lens. The bottom row (orange) is SKiNN: lens mass, lens light, and kinematics parameters feed a network that outputs a vrms velocity image, compared to the kinematic data to give chi-squared_kin. The combined chi-squared_tot is minimized to optimize the whole model jointly. SKiNN replaces only the kinematics piece; the rest of the framework's physics is untouched.

en.text: Why it matters, and where it stops

By turning the slowest step of joint modeling into a cheap forward pass, SKiNN makes it computationally feasible, for the first time, to fit gravitational lensing and spatially resolved kinematics together — and it is precisely the kinematic constraint that corrects the largest source of uncertainty in H0 measurements. The authors are candid about the scope: this is a proof-of-concept. There is no formal ablation table; performance is characterized by the per-pixel error distribution on the test set, the emulator is only valid within the sampled parameter ranges, and the outskirts of the image do carry larger errors.

Perhaps the more transferable idea is the strategy itself: when a model contains an expensive-but-calculable component, you can train a network to emulate that one piece while keeping the surrounding physics intact. You buy the speed of a neural network without giving up the interpretability of the full physical model. That 'replace only the slowest block' pattern seems likely to carry over to many scientific modeling problems well beyond astrophysics.

en.text: Why kinematics modeling is the bottleneck

Spherical Jeans models, the traditional shortcut, are too crude for spatially resolved data and are not self-consistent with the elliptical mass models used in lensing. As instruments like JWST deliver spatially resolved kinematics of lens galaxies, the natural next step is axisymmetric modeling with a code like JAM. But JAM is expensive, and the expense compounds: it lives in the innermost loop of the likelihood evaluation, and an MCMC chain can call that loop hundreds of thousands of times. The cost is not running it once; it is running it again and again.

The key observation is that JAM, though slow, is deterministic and fully calculable. That makes it a good candidate for emulation: generate a batch of JAM outputs, and train a neural network to approximate the mapping. Training is a one-time cost; afterwards each inference is cheap. Importantly, the network does not replace the physics of the overall model — it replaces only the parameters-to-velocity-image computation, while everything around it stays physical.
About 300x faster, at under one percent error

Once trained, SKiNN turns a parameter vector into a velocity image in about 50 milliseconds on a single GPU, against roughly 15 seconds for JAM — about a 300x speedup (and the GPU is itself about 10x faster than a CPU here). The real question is whether that speed costs accuracy. The authors answer it by computing the per-pixel relative error on the 500 held-out test images.

Errors can reach a few percent in the outskirts, but inside the circle they stay below 1% almost everywhere; the histograms on the right confirm that the within-circle relative error concentrates within plus or minus one percent.

en.text: The reading is clear. Errors of a few percent do appear in the image outskirts, but those regions carry little constraining power anyway. In the innermost two arcseconds, where the data actually speaks, the emulation matches JAM to within plus or minus one percent for nearly every pixel. zh.caption: 图1 SKiNN 在联合建模框架中的位置。上半部分（蓝色）是传统透镜建模：用源、透镜质量、透镜光的模型合成一张成像图，与成像数据比对得到 χ²_lens。下半部分（橙色）是 SKiNN：输入透镜质量、透镜光和运动学参数，直接输出一张 vrms 速度图，与运动学数据比对得到 χ²_kin。两者合成的 χ²_tot 被联合最小化，从而对整个模型同时优化。SKiNN 只替换了运动学这一块，框架其余部分的物理保持不变。

zh.text: 意义与边界
SKiNN 把联合建模里最慢的一步换成了一次廉价的前向推理，让引力透镜与空间分辨运动学的联合拟合在计算上第一次变得可行——而正是运动学约束，能纠正 H0 测量里最大的一类不确定性。作者也如实说明了它的定位：这是一个概念验证（proof-of-concept），没有给出正式的消融表，性能由测试集上的逐像素误差分布刻画；仿真只在参数取样的既定范围内有效，外围区域的误差也确实更大。
更值得关注的也许是它背后的思路：当模型里存在“昂贵但可计算”的组件时，可以用一个神经网络仿真这一块，同时把周围的物理原样保留，既借到神经网络的速度，又不牺牲整体模型的物理可解释性。这种“只换最慢的一块”的策略，很可能迁移到天体物理之外的许多科学建模问题上。

Breaking that degeneracy requires an independent constraint — the stellar kinematics of the lens galaxy, essentially how fast its stars are moving.

The problem is that kinematics modeling is slow. To solve the kinematics and the imaging self-consistently, you predict the galaxy's velocity field with a physics code like JAM (Jeans Anisotropic Modeling), and inside an MCMC sampler that code must be recomputed for every single likelihood evaluation. One call takes on the order of fifteen seconds; multiplied over the hundreds of thousands of evaluations a chain needs, jointly exploring the lensing and kinematics parameter spaces becomes computationally prohibitive, so in practice modelers fall back to fitting the two pieces separately. This paper's contribution, SKiNN (Stellar Kinematics Neural Network), targets exactly that bottleneck: train a network to imitate JAM's output, and the slowest step becomes a single forward pass.

en.caption: Figure 1. Where SKiNN fits in a joint modeling framework. The top row (blue) is traditional lens modeling: a model for the source, lens mass, and lens light builds an image that is compared to the imaging data, giving chi-squared_lens. The bottom row (orange) is SKiNN: lens mass, lens light, and kinematics parameters feed a network that outputs a vrms velocity image, compared to the kinematic data to give chi-squared_kin. The combined chi-squared_tot is minimized to optimize the whole model jointly. SKiNN replaces only the kinematics piece; the rest of the framework's physics is untouched.

zh.text: 速度提升 300 倍，精度损失不到 1%
训练完成后，SKiNN 在单块 GPU 上从参数向量生成一张速度图只需约 50 毫秒，相比 JAM 的约 15 秒，大约快了 300 倍（在 GPU 上又比 CPU 快约 10 倍）。真正关键的问题是：这么快，精度还够用吗？作者在 500 张留出的测试图上逐像素计算相对误差来回答。

zh.caption: 图2 两个由 SKiNN 生成的 vrms 图与 JAM 真值的对比。左两列分别是 SKiNN 预测和 JAM 真值，第三列是逐像素相对误差，黑色圆圈标出最内 2 角秒——真实数据约束力最强的区域。可以看到误差在图像外围可能达到几个百分点，但在圆圈内几乎处处小于 1%；最右列的直方图进一步显示，圆内相对误差集中分布在 ±1% 以内。

zh.text: 结论很清楚：图像外围的确会出现几个百分点的误差，但外围本身几乎不受真实数据约束，影响有限；而在最内 2 角秒这个数据真正说话的区域，误差对几乎所有像素都控制在 ±1% 以内。把整张图平均下来，500 张测试图的绝对误差中位数约为 0.47%，第 90 百分位约为 1.1%——两者都明显低于真实速度测量里通常 ≳2% 的系统不确定度。也就是说，仿真带来的误差被真实观测的噪声“淹没”了，不会成为科学结论的主要误差来源。
